verdicts.text: Vault is not open source; it uses the Business Source License model, whereas Pulumi ESC is fully open source and Apache 2.0 licensed.
verdicts.evidence: The core fact holds: GitHub reports the pulumi/esc repo (the CLI/evaluation engine) as licensed "Apache-2.0". Calling ESC "fully open source" goes too far, though. The same page describes ESC as a "Fully managed SaaS service provided by Pulumi Cloud", and that backend is not open source. Vault's move to BSL 1.1 matches public HashiCorp history, but I didn't fetch a source for it in this session.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc (license: Apache-2.0); repo:content/docs/esc/vs/vault.md L27, L52
verdicts.framing_note: overclaim: the source shows 'pulumi/esc repo is Apache-2.0', but the claim says 'ESC is fully open source', which also covers the proprietary Pulumi Cloud service
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Fully open source" for a hosted SaaS product is suspicious. Only the CLI/engine is Apache 2.0.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be composed together from multiple other environments, so shared configuration is inherited rather than duplicated.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README says: "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments." It also says: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration."

verdicts.text: Through Pulumi ESC, secrets stored in Vault can be organized as collections that are versioned, branched, and composed inside other collections.
verdicts.evidence: ESC docs back up "versioned" and "composed": an environment is "a named, versioned YAML document that defines a collection of configuration and secrets", and environments can be composed through imports. "Branched" is weaker. The CLI can `clone` an environment, but the versioning page never mentions branching or forking.
verdicts.source: repo:content/docs/esc/concepts/environments.md L42, L136, L141, L143; repo:content/docs/esc/concepts/versioning.md (no branch/fork/clone match)
verdicts.intuition_flag: ESC has no native branching. "Branched" seems to stretch `pulumi env clone`, which just copies an environment, so the reviewer should decide whether "cloned" is the more accurate word.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is open source under Apache License 2.0; Vault is under Business Source License 1.1 and not open source.
verdicts.evidence: The GitHub API reports the pulumi/esc repo license as "Apache License 2.0" (spdx Apache-2.0). The hashicorp/vault LICENSE file reads "Licensed Work: Vault Version 1.15.0 or later" and "Business Source License 1.1". BSL isn't an OSI-approved open source license.
verdicts.source: gh api repos/pulumi/esc --jq .license; gh api repos/hashicorp/vault/contents/LICENSE
verdicts.framing_note: Two caveats: Vault releases before 1.15 stayed under MPL 2.0, and the Apache 2.0 license covers the open source ESC code, not the hosted Pulumi Cloud service.

verdicts.text: Vault offers a hosted cloud service and self-hosting, and self-hosting requires significant management overhead.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp docs confirm that Vault Enterprise "can also be in a self-managed environment, but is also available as a managed service through the HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP)". Self-managed deployments leave the customer "responsible for the design, deployment, security, reliability, scaling, and upgrading", and HCP is marketed as a way to "Reduce operational overhead". This supports the overhead point, although "significant" is an opinion word.
verdicts.framing_note: "Significant management overhead" is a subjective characterization; the vendor's own docs list the self-managed responsibilities and pitch HCP as reducing that overhead.
verdicts.intuition_flag: HCP Vault Secrets (the SaaS product) reached end-of-life on July 1, 2026, so the hosted option is now only HCP Vault Dedicated. The claim is still true, but any page text naming "Vault Secrets" would be stale.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports pulling secrets from multiple sources including HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, and AWS Secrets Manager; Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC half checks out. pulumi/docs content/docs/esc/providers/secrets/ has provider reference pages 1password-secrets.md, vault-secrets.md and aws-secrets.md, along with azure, gcp, doppler, infisical and aws-parameter-store. I couldn't check the Vault half ("can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault") in the repo, but it fits the fact that Vault has no feature for pulling secrets in from outside stores.
verdicts.intuition_flag: The Vault half is a competitor-positioning claim and too absolute. Vault Enterprise Secrets Sync pushes secrets out to AWS Secrets Manager and other stores, so "can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault" leaves out outbound sync.

verdicts.text: Vault can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault (no open ecosystem of external secret sources).
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's own docs show Vault managing credentials that live in outside systems, not just secrets stored in Vault. Its static roles let Vault rotate existing credentials: "Static credentials are created in the external system first and then added to Vault using an initial credential which is rotated under management." It also generates just-in-time credentials "for popular cloud providers, database platforms, and container orchestration tools," through a pluggable secrets-engine system.
verdicts.intuition_flag: A narrower version would be easier to defend: Vault doesn't natively pull secrets from other secret stores such as AWS Secrets Manager or 1Password, the way ESC does. Saying "can only store and manage secrets stored in Vault" overstates it.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports both a GUI and a Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover, and error checking.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Pulumi's release notes (the ones announcing the "Pulumi ESC Table Editor", i.e. the GUI) say the ESC YAML editor added "auto-complete for faster coding, enhanced diagnostics offering deeper error insights, and hover documentation." The ESC editor enhancements blog post lists Auto-complete, Enhanced Diagnostics and Hover Documentation for the environment editor.
verdicts.framing_note: Source: YAML editor with auto-complete, diagnostics and hover docs, plus a Table Editor. Claim: GUI plus Document Editor with autocomplete, docs hover and error checking.

verdicts.text: Vault's editing is limited: it offers a key/value form editor with a JSON toggle.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's KV v2 tutorial confirms that the Vault UI enters secrets as key/value pairs and has a JSON toggle: "Instead of entering the key-value pairs one by one, you can enter the secret values using JSON." Calling this "limited" is the doc's own comparative opinion, not a falsifiable fact.
verdicts.framing_note: The factual core (a key/value form with a JSON toggle) is confirmed by HashiCorp docs and hashicorp/vault PR #25235. "Limited" is an editorial judgment.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC is available as `pulumi env` in the Pulumi CLI, supports injecting application secrets as environment variables, and supports modifying secrets.
verdicts.evidence: The auto-generated CLI reference lists `pulumi env` ("Manage environments") with subcommands including "pulumi env run - Open the environment with the given name and run a command." (this is how env vars get injected) and "pulumi env set - Set a value within an environment." / "pulumi env edit" (for changing secrets).

verdicts.text: Vault Agent's process supervisor mode can inject secrets as environment variables into a process.
verdicts.evidence: HashiCorp's official docs say: "Vault Agent's Process Supervisor Mode allows Vault secrets to be injected into a process via environment variables using Consul Template markup."
verdicts.framing_note: The claim restates the official docs' description of process supervisor mode, which injects secrets as env vars into the child process named in the exec block.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault have client SDKs.
verdicts.evidence: The public repo pulumi/esc-sdk exists and holds the Pulumi ESC client SDKs. HashiCorp Vault's client libraries are widely known, but I didn't check that half in this session.
verdicts.source: gh search repos esc-sdk --owner pulumi → pulumi/esc-sdk

verdicts.text: Pulumi Service Provider allows management (create, update, delete) of collections of secrets and configuration as a resource; individual Vault secrets can be managed as resources with the Vault provider for Pulumi or Terraform.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi-pulumiservice SDK includes an `Environment` resource (sdk/nodejs/environment.ts). That resource manages ESC environments, which are collections of secrets and configuration, through the normal create/update/delete lifecycle. The pulumi-vault SDK includes the individual secret resources `kv.Secret` and `kv.SecretV2` (sdk/nodejs/kv/secret.ts, secretV2.ts), and pulumi-vault is a bridge of the Terraform Vault provider.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC hierarchical environments inherit values from the environments they import.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc README describes imports as inheritance: "Composable environments: Environments support importing one into another, allowing for easy composability and inheritance of shared secrets and configuration." It also says "Each environment can be composed from multiple environments."

verdicts.text: Vault has no equivalent concept to hierarchical environments; secrets are organized by path convention and the structure is maintained by hand.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) In Vault KV, secrets live at nested paths that you pick to reflect your own structure: "secrets in the form of key-value pairs can be stored at any nested path, allowing to reflect organizational or logical structure." HashiCorp's own docs say namespaces don't share or inherit secrets: "each namespace you created behaves as an isolated Vault environment... no visibility into other namespaces regardless of its hierarchical relationship." So Vault has nothing like ESC's environment imports/composition.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Enterprise namespaces ARE hierarchical (parent/child), but they isolate secrets rather than letting them inherit or compose. "No equivalent concept" holds for inheritance, but a reader could argue namespaces are a hierarchy, so it may be worth rewording to "no inheritance/composition".

verdicts.text: Vault secrets are individually versioned (limited versioning).
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's KV v2 API docs describe versioning per key: "max_versions (int: 0) – The number of versions to keep per key." A secondary guide says the default is 10 versions per secret, which fits "limited versioning". However, KV v1 has no versioning at all, so the claim holds only for KV v2.
verdicts.framing_note: KV v2 docs support per-key (per-secret) versioning with a retention cap. "Limited" is the doc's own comparative wording. The claim leaves out that only KV v2 is versioned, not v1 or dynamic secrets engines.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC allows seeing existing secrets; Vault does not.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's own docs say Vault lets you read the secrets it stores. The kv get docs state: "The kv get command retrieves the value from KV secrets engine at the given key name." So the claim that Vault can't show existing secrets is wrong as written. The table row may mean something narrower, such as viewing secrets held in other external stores, but the line doesn't say that.
verdicts.intuition_flag: It's odd to say a secrets manager can't show existing secrets. The table row (L104-106) probably means a narrower feature and should say which one.

verdicts.text: In Pulumi ESC, environments can import secrets from another environment, and secrets updated in the referenced environment automatically propagate to downstream environments.
verdicts.evidence: The ESC imports concept page says: "Pulumi ESC allows you to compose environments by importing configuration and secrets from other environments" and "The `imports` key is a list of environments that are resolved at runtime." Because imports are resolved at runtime, an update to the imported environment shows up in the environments that import it. One exception: an import pinned to a version tag or revision won't pick up later changes.
verdicts.framing_note: This is backed only by another Pulumi docs page, because the GitHub rate limit blocked a check of the ESC source. Automatic propagation is an inference from "resolved at runtime" and doesn't hold for version-pinned imports.

verdicts.text: Vault has no first-class environment to reference, so secrets are read by path; Vault has no equivalent of secret referencing.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) A 2022 feature request on hashicorp/vault asks for secrets that point to other secrets, and says the workarounds "could be avoided if vault supported secret references." That suggests Vault has no native way for one secret to reference another. Clients read secrets by path, and a HashiCorp forum question from 2024 asking how to do this backs that up.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim names no source. The evidence is indirect: an open-looking feature request, not an official HashiCorp statement. I did not check whether the issue has since been resolved.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports constructing new dynamic values through string interpolation; Vault does not support interpolating values from other values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The ESC half holds up: Pulumi's launch blog says ESC values "can be overridden, interpolated from other values, and arbitrarily nested." The Vault half can't be confirmed as absolute. Vault's KV store doesn't interpolate stored values, but Vault Agent templates (Go templates) can read several secrets and combine them into rendered output. HashiCorp Discuss shows an agent template that merges secrets from paths secret/test1–3 with mergeMap.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Saying Vault "does not support" interpolation goes too far: Vault Agent and consul-template can build values from other secrets on the client side at render time. A qualified wording such as "no server-side interpolation of stored values" would be safer.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC environments can be forked for testing without rewriting entire environments and overriding specific values; Vault does not support branching or personal configs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The ESC half mostly checks out. Pulumi docs say imported values are merged "with the current values overwriting the imported environment's values where keys are redefined", and `pulumi env clone` exists. However, ESC has no feature actually called "fork". I found no authoritative source for the negative Vault half ("does not support branching or personal configs"). It's also arguable: Vault offers namespaces, KV versioning, and templated per-identity secret paths.
verdicts.source: https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/get-started/import-environments/ ; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/iac/cli/commands/pulumi_env_clone/ ; WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC fork environment"
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Forked" isn't ESC terminology (the closest mechanisms are imports+override and clone), and the claim that Vault has no "personal configs" is a sweeping negative. Vault's per-entity templated paths and namespaces arguably cover personal configs.

verdicts.text: `pulumi env diff` shows the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment; Vault cannot compare secrets across environments.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The auto-generated CLI reference confirms the first half word for word: "This command displays the changes between two environments or two versions of a single environment." I found no native Vault command for comparing secrets across environments/paths. However, HashiCorp's KV v2 tutorial says you can "compare the current version to previous ones," and third-party tools (vkv, vault-diff) can compare different secrets, so the absolute "cannot" is only loosely supported.
verdicts.intuition_flag: "Vault cannot compare secrets across environments" is a strong negative. Vault has no built-in cross-path diff, but KV v2 lets you compare versions and third-party tools (vkv, vault-diff) compare secrets across paths. Consider softening to "has no built-in way to diff".

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC supports built-in functions such as `toJSON`, `fromJSON`, `fromBase64`, and `toString`.
verdicts.evidence: The pulumi/esc eval/eval.go source maps `FromBase64Expr -> fromBase64Expr`, `FromJSONExpr -> fromJSONExpr` and `ToJSONExpr -> toJSONExpr`, which confirms fn::fromBase64, fn::fromJSON and fn::toJSON. I didn't see fn::toString in the part of the file I fetched: that code comment doesn't list it, and my later reads were blocked by tool limits. Its presence rests on my recollection that ESC has a ToStringExpr, not on anything I read here.
verdicts.intuition_flag: fn::toString is confirmed only from memory, not from anything fetched. A reviewer should check the ESC built-in functions docs page.

verdicts.text: Vault provides limited templating and transformation functions, such as username templating and the Transform secrets engine, rather than functions for composing configuration values.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) Both named features exist and do what the claim says. Vault's docs say username templating is "used in some secret engines to allow operators to define how dynamic usernames are generated", and the Transform secrets engine encodes and decodes data such as credit-card numbers. Calling these "limited" rather than functions for composing configuration values is a judgment call, not a checkable fact.
verdicts.intuition_flag: Vault Agent templates (consul-template) and Vault Secrets Operator secret transformations ("advanced templating and data filters") can arguably compose configuration values, so "limited" may understate what the wider Vault ecosystem can do.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide audit logs.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Vault docs say: "Audit devices are mountable devices that log requests and responses in Vault." (Note that auditing is off by default until you enable a device.) On the Pulumi side, the pulumi/esc repo README says "All actions taken on environments, secrets, or configuration values are fully logged for auditing."
verdicts.framing_note: No source is cited. The claim holds for both products. One nuance: Vault's audit logging is disabled by default on new clusters.

verdicts.text: Pulumi ESC uses TLS for encryption in transit and unique encryption keys per environment for encryption at rest.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) None of the public sources I found confirm that ESC uses a unique encryption key per environment or TLS in transit. Per-stack unique keys are documented for Pulumi IaC ("For every stack Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key"), and the ESC CMK docs only say "CMKs encrypt data keys, which are used to encrypt secrets in Pulumi ESC", without saying the data keys are per environment.
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Pulumi ESC FAQ \"encryption key\" per environment encrypted in transit"; https://www.pulumi.com/docs/esc/administration/customer-managed-keys/; https://pulumi.com/docs/iac/faq
verdicts.intuition_flag: Wording may be borrowed from the IaC "per-stack unique key" story and applied to ESC environments; the ESC key granularity (per org vs per environment data key) needs to be checked in the product source.

verdicts.text: Vault uses a security barrier for all requests to the backend, which automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit AES cipher in Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's Security Model docs say: "Vault uses a security barrier for all requests made to the backend. The security barrier automatically encrypts all data leaving Vault using a 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) cipher in the Galois Counter Mode (GCM) with 96-bit nonces." Vault's source file barrier_aes_gcm.go agrees: it uses a 12-byte nonce and a 256-bit key.
verdicts.framing_note: The claim restates the HashiCorp passage almost word for word.

verdicts.text: Both Pulumi ESC and Vault provide access controls.
verdicts.evidence: The claim is almost certainly true, but my evidence is indirect. The pricing page says Pulumi Cloud "offers ... RBAC for advanced policy controls" in the Pro edition, but it doesn't mention ESC by name. I couldn't find the ESC access-control page or quote a Vault source because GitHub search hit its rate limit. It is well known that Vault controls access through ACL policies and ESC has environment-level permissions.
verdicts.source: repo:content/pricing/_index.md (L134); gh search blocked by rate limit

verdicts.text: Vault cloud secrets engines generate short-lived credentials for AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, and each engine is configured with a static credential that Vault uses to mint them.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) The first half holds: Vault's AWS, Azure and GCP secrets engines do generate dynamic, short-lived credentials. The second half, that "each engine is configured with a static credential," is wrong as a universal statement. HashiCorp's AWS API docs say root "Credentials can be configured either with IAM access keys for a privileged AWS account, or using Plugin Workload Identity Federation (WIF)." HashiCorp's WIF examples repo says WIF "is available for AWS, GCP, and Azure secret engines and authentication methods" (Vault Enterprise 1.16/1.17+). The AWS engine can also pick up IAM instance-profile or ECS task credentials.
verdicts.framing_note: A static credential is only the traditional/open-source default. WIF (Enterprise) and ambient cloud identity let all three engines run without one. Suggested fix: "typically configured with a static credential (Vault Enterprise supports workload identity federation instead)".
verdicts.intuition_flag: This is a competitor-comparison page, and the claim describes Vault's older setup model while leaving out its newer secretless WIF option.

verdicts.text: Pulumi Cloud can be used as an OIDC provider from the Pulumi SDK, CLI, UI, and pulumi-service provider; configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs say "The Vault OIDC provider feature has a full HTTP API," so the claim that configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is "only available from the CLI" is wrong. Vault's CLI is just a wrapper around that API, and Terraform's vault provider and the Vault UI can also manage OIDC providers (this last part is from general knowledge; the search didn't fetch it). I didn't check the Pulumi half of the claim (SDK/CLI/UI/pulumi-service provider) here.
verdicts.intuition_flag: An "only available from the CLI" claim about an API-first product like Vault is implausible on its face. The Pulumi Cloud half may need a pass1 check against pulumi-service provider source.

verdicts.text: Configuring Vault as an OIDC provider is only available from the CLI.
verdicts.evidence: (escalated from pass1) HashiCorp's docs describe Vault as an OIDC identity provider ("Vault is an OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider"). Every example they give uses the CLI or API (`vault write identity/oidc/...`), but none of the pages I fetched says whether the Vault UI can also configure it. So I couldn't confirm or rule out "only available from the CLI".
verdicts.source: WebSearch ran query "Vault OIDC provider configure UI" and "Vault changelog ui OIDC provider create applications UI 1.11"; https://developer.hashicorp.com/vault/docs/secrets/identity/oidc-provider
verdicts.intuition_flag: I recall, unconfirmed in this session, that the Vault UI added OIDC provider management (Access > OIDC Provider: applications, keys, scopes, providers) around Vault 1.11. If so, "only available from the CLI" is likely out of date. The HTTP API and Terraform are also non-CLI ways to configure it.
